lesson.title: Gaining Ground: What Reduction Really Means
lesson.summary: Reduction is the gain of electrons by an atom, ion, or molecule, which shows up in a formula as a decrease in that atom's oxidation number.
lesson.body:
Reduction completes the OIL RIG mnemonic from the last chapter: Reduction Is Gain, of electrons. The name is even less intuitive than oxidation's, and for a similar historical reason. Metallurgists once used reduction to describe converting a heavy metal oxide ore into the lighter pure metal, literally reducing its mass by stripping away oxygen. The mass connection is gone from the modern chemistry definition, but the word stuck. Today, reduction means only one thing: a species gains electrons.

The same skill you used for oxidation, assigning oxidation numbers, works here too, just in the opposite direction. If an atom's oxidation number goes down over the course of a reaction, that atom has been reduced. A decrease in oxidation number is the fingerprint of a gain in electrons, since each extra electron an atom picks up makes its effective charge one unit more negative.

Return to the magnesium and oxygen reaction from the previous chapter, but now look at the oxygen side. Oxygen gas is reduced to oxide ions: O2 + 4e- is right arrow 2O2-. Check that this half reaction is balanced before trusting it. Atoms: 2 oxygen atoms on the left, in O2, and 2 oxygen atoms on the right, in 2O2-, so atoms balance. Charge: the left side has a neutral O2 molecule plus four electrons, each carrying a charge of -1, for a total charge of 0 + 4(-1) = -4. The right side has two O2- ions, each -2, for a total of 2(-2) = -4. Both sides equal -4, so the half reaction is balanced in both atoms and charge. Oxygen's oxidation number fell from 0, as an uncombined element, to -2, in the oxide ion, a decrease of 2, matching the 4 electrons gained by 2 oxygen atoms, or 2 electrons per atom.

Now place the two half reactions side by side. Magnesium lost 2 electrons per atom, and with 2 magnesium atoms reacting, that is 4 electrons released. Oxygen, as O2, gained exactly those 4 electrons. Nothing was left over on either side. That exact match between electrons lost and electrons gained is not a coincidence in this one example, it is a requirement of every reaction where oxidation and reduction happen together, which is the subject of the next chapter.
